utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I remind you that you are still bound to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth, as you did when you made your declaration at the beginning of the testimony. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you had finished cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, I beg your pardon, Mr. Perovic. I only have a couple of questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, in the course of yesterday's cross-examination, you were asked a question connected to the blockade of barracks of the JNA, of the Yugoslav People's Army by Croatian paramilitary forces. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When were the Yugoslav People's Army's barracks blockaded? When was that? In what period, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened in the spring and summer of 1991, starting sometime in April, 1991, up until the agreement was reached for the barracks to pull out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say in the summer of 1991, did there exist a state of Croatia as an internationally recognised entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It didn't. In fact it did not ask for secession, for simple secession up to the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did that Croatia have a regular armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, it didn't. It only had paramilitary forces, the National Guards Corps and it mobilised its Redarstvenik which is the Croatian term for their police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the only recognised, internationally recognised state in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only internationally recognised state at that time was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did it have its regular armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did. That was the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During cross-examination you were also asked a question related to genocide, namely do you remember the Prosecutor asking you whether top officials of the HDZ in the electoral campaign, which was taking place in 1990 during the first multi-party elections, used the term genocide? Were they threatening the Serbian people with genocide? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And I have a question for you in that connection. Do you have information -- do you know that anyone, while presenting their political programmes wherever and whenever, publicly publicised their intention to commit genocide against a people? Do you know of any such case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions for you. Thank you, Mr. Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is the end of my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just one small question. At page 11, line 1, you mention Colonel Ante Marinov, I believe, a Croat who was dismissed as head of the TO Community of Municipalities. For what reason was that person dismissed? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a JNA Colonel who was committed to the survival of the SFRY and the armed forces, as a member of the armed forces to which he had sworn allegiance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I must be very thick, because I'm still not comprehending the reason. It seems to have eluded me. You seem to be giving me the circumstances, rather than the reason. I would like some help. Any further clarification?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not participate in the creation of a Croatian paramilitary, which was being formed through various clicks through the Territorial Defence, namely the new authorities in Croatia were trying to form it through the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I understand. No more questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Dragisic, you were the commander of the Territorial Defence in Knin at the time when barricades were being set up. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you testified that the barricades were set up because some Croats -- Croatian army were coming to attack the people in Knin. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. The Croatian army was not coming, because Croatia could not have had an army at that time. It was a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the ones who were coming were special Croatian police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Special Croatian police units. Fine. Were coming to attack you people? That was another reason.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now -- and you say that the barricades were then set up by the SDS and the local communities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said also these barricades were unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why would that be allowed? Why didn't the Territorial Defence, of which you were a commander, not do the -- put up the barricades? Why do you allow people to commit -- to break the law and put up barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't and neither could anyone mobilise the Territorial Defence. Only the General Staff, i.e., the president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could do that. Because that is a reserve force. It is not a permanent establishment formation. These were reservists who had their other duties, working in their work organisations or at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were the reservists? Are you saying the Territorial Defence, that you were commander of, is a reserve force? I don't understand. Who is reserve here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was wholly composed of reservists, namely civilians who would at a call up, mobilisation call up they put on their uniforms and repair to their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But isn't it more in line with the law for them to be called up and mobilised rather than just disorganised political parties, SDS as you say, and local communities manned the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be so under normal circumstances, but the circumstances were abnormal, because just as illegally the Croatian police using helicopters, tear gas, and combat armoured vehicles tried to attack citizens who were already in fear, afraid of -- who were already fearing attacks by Croatian paramilitary forces which were being created at the time in contravention of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you're talking about. What would be normal circumstances under which the TO would have been mobilised? I would imagine the TO gets mobilised when an attack is imminent. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a normal situation under which a TO would be mobilised. Now what is so abnormal about this? An imminent attack is there, why don't you mobilise the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, I was not empowered. I am only empowered once mobilisation has been ordered to command such units. I am not empowered to order mobilisation. It was only the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the General Staff of Yugoslavia that were competent to mobilise such units, and no one else was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So until the Presidency has mobilised the TO, you are just sitting ducks. You just sit there and fall for any foreign force to come and attack you. You're not going to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually seek from my superior staff and, in this case it was Colonel Ante Marinov, I inform him about the situation and then he talks to his superiors and that process continues all the way up. I myself cannot order mobilisation in any case, so that was the way it was under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not even suggesting that you should do so. I'm trying to find out why your orders -- I beg your pardon. Your seniors, those who were supposed to make the order, why don't they make that order? Why do they allow an unlawful thing to take place, i.e., barricades set up unlawfully by members of the community? Instead of doing it in a formalised manner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all started because the new Croatian authorities, the party, the Croatian Democratic Union party, in contravention of the constitution and of the law, sought to secede from Yugoslavia and the people from the Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. You're not answering my question. It doesn't matter what motivated the Croatian party to do that. The fact of the matter is an attack is being mounted and, according to you, against your community and your community needs to be defended. It could have been anybody. It could have been Hungary. It could have been Italy attacking you. It doesn't have to have been somebody whose doing it, breaking the law. But the fact of the matter is, there is a physical attack on you and you just sit there and say, okay, fine. The community will defend us. This sounds very bizarre, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dare not undertake any steps and the Presidency of the SFRY and the General Staff on their part were not taking any steps either, that is why the citizens themselves, i.e., the Serbian Democratic Party in Knin, organised the setting up of the barricades in order to block the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question precisely. Why were the authorities not taking any steps? That's my question. Why did they allow the citizenry to break the law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Presidency of the SFRY was composed of nine people, and they could not reach a decision. Half of them were in favour and the other half was against, and therefore such a decision could not be taken. There was also a deadlock in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where was that deadlock? Can you refer us to a meeting where that deadlock was reached?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At meetings, Presidency sessions that were held in Belgrade, there were representatives of every republican province, and the representatives of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia prevented mobilisation from happening and the representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, Vojvodina and Kosovo were requesting mobilisation so that it was half and half and no decision could be reached, and the decision had to be taken by a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did that JNA then begin to get involved in this war without this mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representatives of these republics which I enumerated, namely Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia withdrew from the Presidency and what remained was the so-called rump Presidency and that Presidency was now taking decisions by a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did they withdraw? On what date did they withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They withdrew sometime in autumn 1991, and the then President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They withdrew in autumn 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the barricades were mounted in 1990 before they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the JNA got involved in this war in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did they come in between? Isn't it so that the JNA in 1990 already was forming buffer zones between the warring parties? Was it not so? Or did I mishear? Did I mishear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1990 the JNA did not participate in any way whatsoever in the establishing of buffer zones. The only thing that the JNA was doing was, it was requesting for all paramilitary units to be disarmed. Both Serbian and Croat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did it make that request if the Presidency couldn't agree? There was a deadlock in the Presidency. Obviously if there is no --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They agreed about disarmament, that they agreed. What they couldn't agree about was mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On what day did they agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, a decision was taken sometime in January 1991 for all to return their weapons. And the weapons were returned in Knin, a part of it was returned, because the JNA was threatening that it would be searching and conducting searches and seizing weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on what day was this deadlock where the JNA or the Presidency was unable to decide to mount the barricades because there was a deadlock? When was that? You said earlier that they couldn't decide because -- the JNA couldn't do anything because there was a deadlock. On what day was this deadlock reached?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency would be elected every year from among the ranks of the membership and it was the term of the representative of Croatia to become the president of the Presidency, as a part of the Presidency would not vote for him, he was not appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are not answering my question. I don't care who was going to be the president of the Presidency. I'm saying, on the 18th of July, 1990, when the barricades were being mounted, you say you couldn't mobilise the JNA because there was a deadlock. And I'm saying, when and where was that meeting held on that day, irrespective of who was the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sessions were held for months. They were held for months. The members of the Presidency travelled from one republic to another, without however being able to reach an agreement, for instance in May, June, July, August 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you one question. Just one issue. On what day was this item on the agenda of the Presidency and the Presidency reached a deadlock on it? On what day was that? When they were deciding that they should send the JNA to go and mount barricades in Knin because the Croatian special units are coming to attack and therefore they could not reach agreement, hence the community mounted the barricades? I just want you to tell me when that item was discussed and a deadlock was reached.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but it was sometime in June they still could not reach an agreement. That was in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In June 1991, and the barricades were in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards that particular issue, they couldn't agree at all. Ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On what day did they discuss this issue, sir? Did they ever discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were daily discussions. They were daily sessions held on this topic in the Presidency, but as I said, there was a deadlock in their work. They could not reach any agreement until, in 1991, a part of the members withdrew from the Presidency and went away from Belgrade to their respective republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And why is it that when civilians are breaking the law, they don't get arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on account of the blockade, because Croatia and Slovenia were deliberately violating the constitution, seeking a secession which was not in conformity with the constitution. There was a way the constitution -- they could have asked for secession in, but they wanted to conduct it in a forcible way, namely in contravention of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then if you understood it, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I may have forgotten it or perhaps I may not have understood it. Would you please be so kind as to repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: When the SDS and the community are breaking the law, why don't they get arrested by the Knin police? Why don't they get arrested? You've told us that the mounting of the barricades was unlawful. Why don't they get arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was also unlawful was the attack of the special unit members on the civilian population. And 50 percent of the population participated in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, the second time, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to justify why the SDS and the community did what they did. I'm asking you, why the law enforcement agencies do not arrest them when they break the law.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifty or 100 men cannot arrest 10.000 or 20.000 because the police numbered between 50 and 100 maybe and there were perhaps 20.000 or 30.000 people who came out into the streets in their local communities, who heard over the radio that the state of war was declared, who were expecting an attack, and that same police was also expecting an attack. It wouldn't have been normal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have heard evidence here by other witnesses and I just want you to either confirm or deny it, that in fact when these people had already mounted the barricades, the police then took control and helped them, so that there was order. There was control of the barricades. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened after the 17th, in the next few days the police did not tear down the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't ask you when it happened. My question is, did that happen? Is that evidence correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Now the police, the police associated themselves with this illegal action. Why did they do that? If you say 100 police would not be able to stop 20.000 people, why then do they join them and associate themselves with the illegal action instead of distancing themselves from it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was also a part of the people, a part of that same citizenry of that same community. And as to your interpretation of unlawfulness, the police complied with the law of the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was the only existing entity. The police could not conform with the law of a non-existing state, at least not yet existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. If you say my interpretation of unlawfulness. That is not my interpretation. You told me -- I asked you right at the beginning. You said that it was unlawful what the people did. So unlawfulness is your interpretation. I'm following on what you are telling me, okay. I have expressed no interpretation of anything here. I'm just asking you questions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now on your interpretation of unlawfulness, why did the police associate themselves with this unlawful act; that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they could not act otherwise, they were just as much in jeopardy as we, the people. All of us were in danger. Since mobilisation of the armed forces could not be carried out, that was the only way to prevent conflict and to protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Martic's attitude was to these barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Martic held the same view. He thought it was the only way to protect the people and the police force from a clash with Croat's special units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Perovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, did you, as the commander of the Knin Territorial Defence, have legal authority to order a mobilisation of the personnel in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who had such authority to issue that kind of order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY or the General Staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the first time when the Yugoslav People's Army intervened to create a buffer zone, as you put it? Do you remember in which period that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in autumn 1990 or maybe even later. Yes, it was later. In the spring of 1991. Yes, I remember now. The first time the JNA established a buffer zone in Plitvice after the skirmish between the police of Krajina and the Croatian police, which means after the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to follow up on the question asked by His Honour, Judge Moloto, why were not the people who organised and manned the barricades arrested? I haven't finished my question. Do you have any knowledge where the people who illegally smuggled arms from Hungary were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were those who imposed blockades on JNA barracks and installations arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So those who illegally smuggled arms into Croatia were not arrested? And those who attacked the Yugoslav People's Army were not arrested either? And those who manned the barricades were not arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Also very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, just a couple of more questions. You mentioned a SFRY Presidency session which you talked about the deadlock was reached. That was on the 12th of March, 1991, does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm telling you I can't know for sure, because those attempts to reach an agreement within the Presidency lasted for months. I believe that Mr. Jovic probably has the date in the book that he has written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And if I told you that this date of the 12th of March 1991 came from Jovic's book, that would probably be an accurate date, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just so that I am clear on it. So this was many months after the erection of the barricades in August of 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also, in response to a question from His Honour Judge Moloto, you said that in 1990 the JNA did not participate in any way whatsoever in the establishing of buffer zones. The only thing that the JNA was doing was, it was requesting for all paramilitary units to be disarmed. Did you know that even before the barricades Borisav Jovic had pledged that the JNA would support and protect the political ambitions of the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but Mr. Jovic probably wrote about that. I personally was not involved in politics and I haven't read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you -- you yourself said that as far as you know or as far as you believe, JNA planes turned back some Croatian, I believe, helicopters you said on the 17th of August, 1990, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if that's true, that would certainly constitute some sort of JNA activity with regard to the conflict, separate from requesting that paramilitaries be disarmed, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the JNA was the only one authorised to issue approvals for helicopter sorties and the helicopters in question took off without the approval of the JNA and that's why they were prevented from flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually another question about the SFRY Presidency sessions. You talked about how some members left the Presidency and returned to their own republics. And I believe this was around March. It was actually Jovic, the Serbian representative, who first left the Presidency and then he at some point came back; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who first left the Presidency, who first walked out, because they were constantly in deadlock. As I explained a moment earlier, half of them was in favour of one option, and the other half was in favour of the opposite, so they were not able to function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether -- I don't know whether you are satisfied with the answer given to your question at page 17, line 1. I'm particularly interested to hear that correct -- an appropriate answer to that question. The question was: And if that's true, that would certainly constitute some sort of JNA activity with regard to the conflict separate from requesting that paramilitaries be disarmed, right? The answer doesn't sort of address that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, you've heard His Honour's comments. Could you, could you respond to that question. This turning back of the helicopters that you said happened on the 17th of August, 1990, that would constitute some form of JNA intervention, separate from this issue of disarming paramilitaries, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a regular activity of the JNA. The JNA was authorised, the only one authorised to issue approvals for helicopter flights. These flights of the Croatian police were neither announced, nor approved. So the JNA acted in conformity with the law and it would have acted the same way if those flights were made by anyone else. Because the JNA was the only regular lawful armed force in that state. The JNA was not only Serb. It was also Slovene and Croatian and officers, as you saw from the example of Mr. Marinov, Colonel Marinov, came from all ethnic groups, all nationalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may proceed Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic, do I understand you correctly that according to you, the JNA had to approve every single helicopter flight, in the entire SFRY in the entire Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did that work? Can you explain a little bit how that approval system worked, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every republic there existed an army district, military district with its own army command. And one part of each command was in charge of air space, all flights had to be announced, all flight plans had to be submitted and the command had to issue their approval for the flight. Because the army also had air defence units, these units had to know about the flights, so as to avoid friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And that was true for every helicopter flight, emergency medical evacuations, police helicopter flights, every kind of -- every kind of flight in the airspace had to be approved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. One last question for you. And it's again about the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's again about the SFRY Presidency sessions. Croatia and Slovenia continued to participate in those Presidency sessions until the fall of 1991, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Thank you, sir. This brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to say thank you to you for taking the time off to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry, sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry and I'm sorry, Your Honour. I hate to be a pest, though some might say that is part of the job of a Prosecutor. But yesterday, just to take up this issue again of the filing of the 92 bis or 89(F) motion, I understood Defence counsel to say yesterday that they could indicate to us, today, this morning, when they might be able to file a motion with respect to the first batch. So I just wonder if we could take a moment to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not being a pest, you are just being, being my memory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to give an indication to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have begun to work on those submissions and I now have a problem. Should I reply to the Prosecutor about all statements? Or just the first batch? As for the first batch, it should be there just after this first break. Just after the first break -- I believe we have a break after this Monday from the 29th, right? So those statements should be submitted to the Chamber around the 1st. I was talking about the break, we will not be here from the 25th until the 29th, and after that we should have those statements. Let us say around the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of October? Mr. Whiting, 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The 1st is actually a Sunday, but I suppose the 2nd of October. That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will be the 2nd of October, then, Mr. Milovancevic, because the 1st is a Sunday. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please usher in Mr. Plejo Stevo; that is Stevo, first name, Plejo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Plejo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before I begin my examination-in-chief, I have a request. Please, we really must make a brief pause between questions and answers to enable the interpreters to do their job. Could you please, for the record, give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevo Plejo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th of June, 1964, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What's your ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb, Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were born in Knin. Tell us about your schooling.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the school of mechanical engineering in 1983, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you find employment and where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, 1985, after I did my military service, I found a job in a bolt and screws factory in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say you found a job in '84?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1985, in a factory called Tvik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you found a job in a factory in Knin. Since you were employed and lived there, could you tell us, what were interpersonal relations like at that time, as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you mean between ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any conflicts and I didn't hear of any conflicts on ethnic grounds. There were never any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said there had been no conflicts, but how would you describe the relations among people. Were they chilly, or were they decent, were the ethnic groups separated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no separation. People intermingled, and I personally socialised with people of other ethnic groups and religions. We worked together and we were even friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said "we were even friends." Would it be fair to say that interpersonal relations were normal, human, friendly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How large is the factory that employed you? How many people did it employ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the employees of one ethnicity only, or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were Serbs, because the majority of the population was Serb, but there were Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We just talk about interpersonal relations in villages and towns. What were intra-ethnic relations in workplaces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in my factory. They were ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said "they were ideal." Did that come to an end at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not until the very end, not until they abandoned the factory and the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say "they" abandoned the factory and the municipality of Knin. Who is "they"? When did "they" leave and why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "they", I mean Croats. Very simply one day they just didn't show up for work, not a single one of them. Until the day before we had worked together. We had coffee breaks together and the next day they didn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I please interrupt you at this point. Can you tell us at least roughly, how many Croat employees were there in your factory, Tvik? You said they had just stopped coming to work one day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know in the section where I worked, that employed mainly younger people, that is my age, and we went on coffee breaks together and I didn't even know what their ethnicity was always. But as far as those I know are concerned, I know were Croats, they just didn't show up for work one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people you knew were Croat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my section, around ten, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or did you learn why they did not show up for work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I didn't know. However, since I lived halfway between two municipalities, Knin and Drnis, and Knin was at the time under Croatian control, I mean it was a majority Croat place, I ran into one of those men wearing a uniform of the new Croatian police. And I learned that they had been given instructions to leave Knin, that they would be given new jobs immediately. But in those days, although we watched Croat TV and we didn't hear any reports about somebody being driven out, I just concluded that they had left of their own will and joined the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when those employees of the Tvik factory, who were Croats, stopped their employment there, moved away and joined the Croatian police, can you tell us, what was the situation generally in Croatia and in your community?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, tensions were already somewhat high. It was quite clear that the Croatian state wanted to secede from the then Yugoslavia and relations became increasingly tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did this mounting of tensions occur? How was it manifested? How could it be seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was evident in evidence from what the mass media were carrying and also people were talking about it, it being quite evident that Croatia wished to secede from the rest of Yugoslavia, i.e., from the existing state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any political events at that time? Did they play any role?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what specifically you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant political gatherings of parties, were there any such gatherings characterising the period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the term "barricades" ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that means for you, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricades were mainly set up between territories where the majority Croat, i.e., Serb population, because rumours were spreading and the Croatian television was also saying that Croatia would be entering Serbian municipalities, disarming the police, installing some emblems which to us, people of Serb ethnicity, had always been Ustasha emblems, the chequer-board flag and such. So that the people spontaneously put up these barricades as a form of defence against possible violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I couldn't understand the beginning of the answer. He says -- it may be an interpretation problem. "The barricades were mainly set up between territories where the majority Croat, i.e., Serb population." I don't understand that part. And then "because rumours were spreading." From "because" it didn't even relate to what he said at the beginning. Can we just clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You heard the question of His Honour, Judge Moloto. You mentioned the location of the barricades, and you spoke about a majority Croat populated, and a majority Serb populated territory. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't express myself properly. The people were erecting these barricades spontaneously. At times this would not be a barricade between such territories. Sometimes people just erected barricades in their villages, because they expected that they might come under attack. So it wasn't the rule to place barricades between Croat and Serbian places or towns. Sometimes they would be put up even between two Serbian places, because the objective of the people was to protect their homes with the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that is the end of 1990, early 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So they set up barricades, and you described that for us. Were there any armed conflicts at the time when the barricades were being put up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there had been any armed conflicts before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there was any armed conflict or what was the first time that you heard about any armed conflicts there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Plitvice clash. That was the first one that I heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was and what was it about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was in March 1991, although I don't remember dates very well, and was not that much interested in dates. I believe it was March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about the Plitvice clash, from whom and how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, in fact, a couple of my friends or neighbours from the place, from my place were also at Plitvice. And they were on the Krajina police force. So they had been police members from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until which time did you remain working in the bolts and screws factory in Knin. You say that you remained there until 1985 [as interpreted]. Until which time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime until March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in March 1991? I mean with relation to your employment, to your job.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after these events, perhaps it was the beginning of April, I got an oral summons from Mr. Milan Martic to come and join the reserve force of the militia of the SAO Krajina, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say you were orally invited. Did Mr. Martic actually know you? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I knew him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This may be an interpretation issue but I think the witness said he received an oral summons, not that he was orally invited. And there may be a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript says "summons," Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I thank the Prosecutor for his intervention. The witness said that he was orally invited by Mr. Martic. And we shall clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you why you had left your job, what did you say, Mr. Witness, can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was orally invited by Mr. Martic to join the reserve force of the militia of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this okay now, my learned colleague, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to say about it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But can we ask him, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me say this, Mr. Milovancevic. It becomes very problematic, because before you asked the witness to clarify, you clarified. So the witness has nothing to say but to say what you told him. And this is what I've been trying to warn you against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are quite right. I am remiss, but this was inadvertent on my part, because I heard the witness, who replied the way he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you heard him, then don't repeat after him. Ask him to clarify, because we don't understand, and you see this "remiss" is happening a little too often, Mr. Milovancevic. That's my problem. Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, you worked in the bolts and screws factory until May, 1991. Did you change jobs after that, your employment, work post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was invited by Mr. Milan Martic to join the reserve police force of the SAO Krajina at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you join it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean when you say that you joined the reserve force? I mean, in terms of employment. Does that imply anything in terms of employment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remained an employee of the factory. I remained employed at the factory and, according to our rules, one could be a member of the reserve police force or an army reservist if one was able and fit. One had to be on a reserve force, it was just a question of which one it would be, the army or the police reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you accepted to join the reserve police force, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was then issued with equipment, arms and uniforms and for a while I was assigned to the territory in which I lived, doing routine duties, traffic control, controlling the situation generally and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the uniform that you were issued with at that time, what colour was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was blue, a blue uniform, just the way it used to be, the way the standard militia, the police uniforms were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say you were issued with a uniform, weapons and you were assigned your work tasks. Until which time did you perform such tasks as a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until -- so this was in April, so I did that work, if you are referring to the duties I performed where I lived, that was until around May, 1991. It may have been -- maybe the 15th or the 20th of April. In fact, no, it was earlier, or rather, I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was for a brief time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just prior to the break, what happened after these 20 or so days? Was there any change? You say that you worked as a policeman, and after that what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the youth settlement in Golubic which is a place near Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called via radio communications, via the radio which I had in my car. I was to report there to the command there, and to leave my car there. And I was to report to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We shall deal with that question after the break. And Your Honours, I believe that this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at quarter to eleven. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, maybe just before you proceed, can I just ask one little question. Witness, just before we went for the break, you indicated that you went to Golubic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you asked to go to Golubic by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said one of the commanders of the police station in Knin told me that I was to bring back and return my vehicle to where I had been before that, and then to report to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that your personal vehicle or was it a government vehicle, a police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Responding to the earlier question, you said that you became a member of the reserve force of the police. To what particular station did you belong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that after some 20 days, you had returned your service vehicle and then went to Golubic, can you tell us what the purpose of that was? What were you told?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me nothing. They just said that I should report to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you came to Golubic, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There I was met by a commander, his name was Dragan Karina. I believe that he was an inspector, and he was my commander there. He met me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in Golubic after arriving there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well at that particular time, nothing special. Nothing in particular. We just played some soccer. Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Golubic and after you had been met by the inspector who you said was your commanding officer, were you given any training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially not. Only fitness training, in the beginning, which was running and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were there attending the fitness training and how old were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These why all youngish people, between 20 and 30 years of age. I cannot say whether they were perhaps 40 of them. Possibly their number was around 40. I'm not quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did this period last of fitness training in Golubic and your playing of football as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for several days, perhaps five -- six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Did anything change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, a certain man came and our commanding officer introduced him to us as Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was Captain Dragan's job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our commander told us that he was a capable man, a professional and that he would be giving us some police training, which we accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that training with Captain Dragan indeed carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did that training consist of? What was it that you were taught by Captain Dragan in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would call it classical police training, which consisted of securing persons. We were trained how to secure persons, and also if for instance someone shot at this important person, how he was to be protected. Then how to protect ourselves against terrorists, against knives, against pistols, fitness training, descending a rope on a rock face and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You called this police training. Can we call it, perhaps, specialist -- special unit training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would call it classical police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long -- how much did this training last with Captain Dragan, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted for around 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During those 20-odd days, were you issued any orders to go out in the field? Did you have such situations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What occasion was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once -- one night some civilians in Knin tried to burgle some shops, some outlets which were in the ownership of Croatian firms, so we were ordered at around 2300 or 2400 hours to get quickly dressed and to go and intervene on the spot. So we sat in our cars and arrived in Knin. We were not wearing any arms, but just the rubber batons that we had been issued with, and because some people were burglarising some of these outlets, we were to go to the scene and intervene. But the regular police that was in the police station had already put things under control and had apprehended the people who tried to do that so that there was no need for us to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you return to Golubic after that? I'm sorry. After receiving that information, did you go back to Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we returned to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While the training was in process in Golubic, did you wear any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We wore blue service police uniforms, top and the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any insignia, any markings on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the sleeve there was a patch with the words "the militia of the SAO Krajina" inscribed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the basic colour of the uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the training with Captain Dragan lasted for 20 days. What happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, other people came and I assessed -- in fact, I didn't assess, I was told that these people are mainly from the Knin municipality, from Benkovac, I believe. The idea was to set up a unit of between 20 and 30 people from each municipality, so that people from these other municipalities came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many of those people came?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the number. Perhaps another 60 or 70 people, 20 from each municipality or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you -- with you, after this training was completed? Did you remain in Golubic? Did you leave Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained in Golubic and we were supposed to pass on the knowledge we had obtained at the training course from Captain Dragan and our commanding officer. We were supposed to transmit it to these other people from these other municipalities, to pass on what we had learned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also undertake that task?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair for me to say that you were actually an instructor at this course?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hold any rank? Did you have any other function or any -- or any other role?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I and some of my colleagues were given the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were conferred the rank of lieutenant, for what unit -- of what unit were you lieutenant? Excuse me. Was it the police? Was it the Territorial Defence, the army, or something else? That is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As an instructor, how large was the group that you were in charge of, or rather, the group that you trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 30 and 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this training that you were now delivering to the new trainees, was it different in content from what you learned from Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't different in content. What else could we pass on but what we had learned from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the training, did you go out in the field to undertake some training exercises in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion we went to Udbine to carry out training, it was the same thing but on another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say we went up there to Udbine, can you tell us where Udbine is, between what and what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Lika, maybe 30, 40 kilometres away from Knin. It's a small townlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So where in Udbine did you have this drill? Outdoors? Indoors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outdoors. On the outskirts of Udbine, we didn't want to go into the populated centre where there were people. We went to the periphery, five, 600 kilometers -- metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you scheduled to stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long we were scheduled to stay there, but I believe we were thrown out I believe by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain that? "I think we were thrown out by the then army?" Which army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still the Yugoslav People's Army and on one occasion two officers, two ranking officers of the JNA came and asked us to withdraw immediately to go back to Knin, and if we didn't, they would use force. That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did those ranking officers of the JNA introduce themselves? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not, but they said they were from the 5th Army District, which was the Zagreb army district. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did you respond to their demand that you withdraw and the threat of force? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within our unit there was one man in charge of communications, so we told him to report the latest developments to the headquarters in Knin. I don't know to whom he talked in Knin, but I believe he informed the commanders in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that? How was this problem in Udbine resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself, but I heard that Mr. Martic had come, together with Milan Babic, I believe, and they had some sort of negotiations with the army officers and we indeed went back to Knin, maybe the same day, maybe the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they come to Udbine, did Mr. Martic and Mr. Milan Babic come to Udbine to come and negotiate with the police officers while you were there during your exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Despite these negotiations that Mr. Babic and Mr. Martic had with the army officers, you said that you returned to Knin the next day. Does that mean that the negotiations failed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend them myself. I suppose they failed, since we had to return before we were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To understand that, may I, Mr. Milovancevic, ask further questions? So that was negotiations between Mr. Martic and Mr. Babic on the one side, and the JNA officers on the other side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And first, when the JNA people met you and said you shouldn't be there, how many JNA persons were that? What size of a group was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that specific place where we had our office, two officers came. One was lieutenant colonel and another one did not have any rank insignia, but the army was based on the periphery of Udbine anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. And you had sort of an office there, is that right? Because first I understood that you were there only one day in Udbine. And now you used the word or in the translation I understood you had an office there set up, some sort of an office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had been there for several days. It was not just one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The training was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You took a group there, or there was a larger group? How many about, from Golubic, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, between 30 and 40 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: He has not in fact responded as to how many JNA persons were there, has he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I understood there was two, and the army in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And this place that your office was in the surrounding areas of this village, it was about half a kilometre from the village, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This very spot is on an elevation. It's a small place. It's clearly visible -- I mean visibility is very good both there and all around. So those two officers came perhaps with a driver to see us, but the army was based very near this little town, so we could see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. That's okay. And did we get the name of that town right, is it Udbine? Is that correct? And Udbine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Udbine. U-D-B-I-N-E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's in the transcript we -- until so far, didn't have it. Is this a Croatian or Serb or mixed town? Do you happen to know that, to ask a last question on that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it's majority Serb place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry for interrupting and you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke a moment ago about completing that course, and then taking over a group of men to train, as an instructor, as their commander. Was that the only group that you led in training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a rough timeline, what part of the year was that? A month at least if not a date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been May or June, 1991. May, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in Golubic, do you remember if there was any incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no incidents. In fact, I heard of an incident, but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is it exactly that you heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that some Croats, a few Croats had been captured, and that one of my colleagues, commanders, who was passing through slapped those Croats about. Slapped their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did that cause any kind of reaction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was at home leaving Knin on that day and my colleagues told me later that Captain Dragan had summoned Mr. Martic and told him, how long are we going to tolerate things of this kind? If we go on like this then everything is pointless. And he told him in conclusion that such things must not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were told this by your colleagues who were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Milovancevic. What are these things that Mr. Martic was asked how long they should be tolerated for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat? I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said "I think I was at home leaving Knin on that day, and my colleagues told me later that Captain Dragan had summoned Mr. Martic and told him, how long are we going to tolerate things of this kind? If we go on like this, then everything is pointless. And he told him in conclusion that such things must not happen." What are these things that he was not prepared to tolerate which must stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Dragan probably did not have the authority to expel that man, so he invited Mr. Martic and he explained to Mr. Martic that that commanding officer had slapped about the captives. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he invited Mr. Martic and told him what had happened. Mr. Martic, of course, himself, was not willing to tolerate such things and he expelled this commanding officer immediately, told him to return his equipment to supplies, and to leave immediately. I mean, this commander who had done this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was Mr. Martic at that time? Why was Mr. Martic able to expel this person? What authority do he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at that time Mr. Martic was the secretary of the SUP, the secretariat of the interior. I'm not quite sure but I believe he was the secretary of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And as such, did he have authority over Golubic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry, before you go on, Mr. Milovancevic. Other than this instance, were there other instances of abuse by your colleagues? Because you seem to have given your evidence in a manner that indicates that it wasn't a singular incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said there was only one incident, and I related that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. But you said, Mr. Dragan said "how long are we going to tolerate these things?" It looks like these things had been happening and they are getting out of hand. That's the basis of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. The evidence is: How long are we going to tolerate things of this kind? So you speak of a state of affairs that had built up, which Dragan was not accepting, or happy with, and that he wanted to bring these things to summon Mr. Martic and see that they were addressed. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, either I didn't express myself very well, or it was not properly interpreted. Before that incident, there were no captives. No one was captured, and there were no incidents. That was the first case. So Captain Dragan called Mr. Martic and told him, can we tolerate this? Martic said, of course not. And he expelled that commander immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So were there other incidents, if that was the first case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were no other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you conducted another course. How long did that second course take?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, 20 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the trainees trained for? To be aware and do what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We imparted to them the same training that we had received earlier, and as far as I remember, the plan was for them to be within the police force in their own municipalities, to be trained for the same jobs, VIP security or personal security and maintaining law and order, the things I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. The trainees in the second course that you trained, did they stay in this centre in Golubic or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they returned to their respective municipalities. I have no idea what they did later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that centre in Golubic, there were reserve policemen and policemen. Was there anyone else, apart from them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no other people. In fact I don't know who you mean specifically by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant Territorial Defence, the army, JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I mentioned the old Knin Hospital, would that ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I worked after these events, and that's where the district prison of Knin was later established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you worked in the area at some point. Were you then a reserve policeman of the Knin SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for another ten days, or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how did you come to be engaged in that job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of men from the Golubic centre, maybe 15 or 20, together with their commander, were sent to secure the premises and to transfer the detainees to that part of the old hospital where the conditions were better. The hospital was mostly in disuse, but there was one part still functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You're now talking about the old hospital. Can you tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what was the task of these men?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
