utterances.text: Their task was to transfer those same Croats that we mentioned earlier to the still functioning part of the old hospital, and to provide them with everything that was necessary until a better solution was found, such as an exchange or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go into that old hospital in Knin? Can you describe those premises? How large was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When that group of men left, I myself came there three or four days later and this commander who had the task of improving the conditions there complained to Dragan Karina in Golubic that he couldn't do it all himself, there were window panes shattered, doors broken. There was no hot water. I don't even know whether there was cold water. That he had to provide security on top of all of that and that he just couldn't manage all on his own. So the commander told him to see me, if I can help with the job. So three or four days later, I joined him there and tried to do whatever is necessary to put the place in order so that it could be fit for placing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, the man who was sent to the old hospital to restore it to some habitable condition couldn't manage and he came back to the commander to complain and the commander then assigned you to help him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What needed to be done at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what I said a moment ago. I first listed all the things that were broken or in disrepair. I saw to it that the window panes were replaced, the doors reinstalled, to provide bedding. Everything that is necessary for people to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that a part of the old hospital in Knin was used as a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many rooms were used for that? I suppose there is some sort of lobby, corridor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rather large building, consisting of two parts, two wings. The right wing was more recent and it was in better condition and it was the rooms in the right wing that we used. I believe there were four or five rooms, maybe two lavatories, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So when you came there four our five days later, after that group, and the man in charge of the group complained that he couldn't manage on his own, so you were sent to help him, so when you arrived there, what did you find in the rooms? Were there any beds or ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were no beds. There were only mattresses, three-piece military mattresses. I mean when I say military it is not exactly precise. I don't know to whom they belonged, but I know it is the type of army issue three-piece mattress that I slept on while I was in my police training or in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the size of the rooms? How many mattress were there? How many people could you place in one room?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not all the same size. There were smaller and larger rooms, but they were mostly the ward-type of rooms, with rather high ceilings, and there was no need to put many people in one room. We had just ten or so captured men and the -- we could place them in a couple of rooms and the rest of the rooms could stay empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said there were about ten people. How many captives were there at the time? Were they captives?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Captives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a bathroom, a lavatory in the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the wash basins and toilets? In the rooms or outside?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a corridor. The rooms were on the right side of the corridor, and on the left side there were bathrooms and lavatories and maybe some auxiliary rooms such as pantries or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So did the captives have access to the bathrooms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they receive food? Was it organised? Or did they have to make do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Food supply was organised. They ate the same food that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many men secured this hospital that was now used as a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 to 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did they guard? Where they were -- were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large building, so there were three guard posts, two at the gates and one more outside. It was important for us to provide security outside, so that nobody could enter, enter from the street, because we were in the very centre of town. And there was a couple of other guard posts inside where security men would monitor movement and let people in and out of the lavatories, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said the security detail was deployed outside. It was a large building, there were a couple of entrances. Did they secure the prison alone or were there any other buildings around?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had on-the-job occupational, medical centre. And just next to us some sort of infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that one part of the building was used for providing occupational medical care, and you used the other part as a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How exactly did you make sure that there would be no unauthorized access?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We placed guards on the gates and it was possible to ensure security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay with this detail in the old hospital, together with that group that you came to assist.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group was there for a very short time, maybe ten days, or so, and then they left. And members of the Territorial Defence later came to replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To what Territorial Defence did those Territorial Defence members belong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mainly from Knin. I knew them all. They were between 40 and 50 years of age. They had not been mobilised into the army and they belonged to the Territorial Defence. Of course I didn't know who would be assigned to the Territorial Defence or to the army, but those were mainly elderly people from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When they came, did these men who were there before withdraw, all of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of them withdrew, except for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During the stay of this first group, the first ten days when they were making, so to speak, that prison, what was their attitude and their treatment of the prisoners and what was yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. What do you mean "when they were making that prison"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was describing how a group of people was given the task of adapting some parts of the old hospital to serve as a prison, so that I conditionally called that process in the physical sense the making of a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think that's a correct characterisation. I think it was just the repairs to the prison. When you say "making of a prison," it looks like it is being started and it will be used after it has been made. But from this witness's testimony, people were there before the repairs were made. Captives were kept there before the repairs were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We shall clear this up, if you allow, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the second group completed its training in Golubic, a smaller group was assigned the task of adapting the old hospital to be used as a prison. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the captive Croats had been kept until that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- well, the question is superfluous at this point -- whether they were kept in the rooms which were adapted to that purpose? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you, Your Honours, have any question in connection with this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, because I think you are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you are giving it a different slant from what I think this witness has told us so far. Let me just go back to what he said earlier. You said to us, you heard that some Croats had been captured and that one of your colleagues, a commander, who was passing through slapped those Croats. Okay, wait a minute. That's going too far. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is page 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 44? Thank you very much. You said, sir: "A number of men from the Golubic centre, maybe 15 or 20, together with their commander were sent to secure the premises and to transfer the detainees to that part of the old hospital where the conditions were better. The hospital was mostly in disuse, but there was one part still functioning." Now from that, is it fair to infer that before this 15 and 20 people went there to repair the hospital, there were detainees there in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's our deduction from what you say. You're saying they were sent to secure the premises, and to transfer the detainees to that part of the old hospital where the conditions were better. So they must have been in a part of the hospital where conditions were not better. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not so, Your Honours. I said that those people, that commander with some 15 to 20 people had been sent to take the detainees from Golubici to the -- to the part of the hospital which had slightly better conditions than the other section. The other section had been abandoned some eight years ago and it was totally inhabitable, so there were two wings, two parts. When I say the old hospital, there was this left wing and there was the right wing. The right wing was built much later, and the conditions in it were slightly better than in the left wing. That is why they chose the right wing, because it was a bit more decent. There was water, et cetera, whereas in the left part, there was no water, no electricity, no conditions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also said -- let me tell you what you also said: "That their task was to transfer those same Croats, that were mentioned earlier, to the still functioning part of the old hospital, and to provide them with everything that was necessary until a better solution was found, such as an exchange or something." That's what you said. What you are now telling us is a complete change from what you told us earlier, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not different, Your Honours. I really said the same thing. Perhaps you understood me differently. Those people from Golubic, this group, should I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's the person who interprets for us. I am reading what is written here. I am quoting. I'm not paraphrasing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But actually it wasn't mentioned at all where these detainees came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Where these detainees were transferred from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He never mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was not mentioned and we understood it from another part of the building, but it was from another place and that was the original place that was Golubic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's telling us about Golubic as a place from where the detainees were being transferred for the first time now. We never heard Golubic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes -- no. It was open. It was not being said, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. I beg your pardon. This witness said -- this witness said, that they were sent to secure the premises and to transfer the detainees to that part of the old hospital where the conditions were better. And he later says: Their task was to transfer those same Croats that were mentioned earlier to the still functioning part of the old hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe can you clarify it by asking -- by answering the following question. Before you worked on the repair of these premises, were there any detainees in the building, in the whole building of the old hospital? And then you repaired that and only later you were involved in the transfer of the detainees? Or did you transfer them and repair that at the same time, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I was quite precise. I came to two or four days after the rest of the group had arrived, so earlier there were no captives. There had been no prisoners at all. Those were the first people who were taken prisoner maybe on that very same day. So when this group was sent with the prisoners, from Golubic, because in Golubic there were no conditions where to place them, they took them to -- put them in the old hospital building. Now, in the old hospital building, they opted for the right wing, which was in better shape than the left wing of that old hospital. I believe that I clearly said that. In fact, there had been no prisoners at all before that. 1991

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. But what we want to know and what I got from you, had you completed the repair process and improvement process before those prisoners, who were taken and detained on the said day, before they were put into the detention facility? Had you completed the process of improvement and repair at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were four or five rooms there. Two were habitable and we could put the prisoners there. A lot of work needed to be done on the other ones. Hot water needed to be installed. Some windows needed to be glazed. Doors needed to be replaced but they were already staying there. They had been staying there for a couple of days before I arrived there, but there needed -- more work needed to be done anyway, in order to create the best possible conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the point we are making. They were there before the repairs were done. This is what you're telling us now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why does it take you so long to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I replied immediately, but perhaps I was not properly understood. I sought to be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've been saying, these people were transferred from the one part of the hospital that was bad to a better part. You say, no, no, no, they came from Golubic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So how long had they been there before the repairs we're affected? In the hospital? How long were they in the hospital before the repairs we're affected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After these prisoners had been sent from Golubic, escorted by this group of guards, a couple of days later, two or three days later when this commanding officer complained to me that much more work needed to be done, I immediately went there. So that they had been staying there for only two or three days, in this right wing of the hospital after coming from Golubic. They never stayed in the left wing. They were in the right wing where the conditions were better, for a couple of days. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: During the repair works, what did you do with the inmates? Did you transfer them into -- into a different room? Would that clarify that also? But I don't want to interfere too much. Exactly what I also didn't really understand, what did you do with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were three or four or five rooms there. We chose the one with the best conditions, with glazed windows, where there was no draft and where the conditions were generally better. So we would place them in that room in order to carry out repairs in the next room. And then we would distribute them to the next room, which was repaired so as not to keep all of them, 20 or 30 of them, in one room. So as this process of repairs unfolded, we would transfer them from one to the next room, because we had no other place to put them. Our problem was that prior to the war, there didn't exist a prison in Knin, so that we had to act quickly. And then I also forgot to add something, but I will say that later, possibly to a question of relevance; namely, I wanted to say also that, at that time, we already had not only Croats as prisoners, we already had -- we had Serbs, who were answerable for criminal offences and we had to give some thought to where we would be placing the Serbs, too, when they were -- when they had committed a criminal offence. It was not only a question of the placement of war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So the Croats that you had there, what type of prisoners were they? Were they prisoners awaiting trial? Or prisoners who were war criminals or detained as having been captured? What type of prisoners were the Croats as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we understood them to be prisoners of wars because, in previous incidents at Plitvice for instance, many Serbs had been captured, and all requests for them to be released had been refused. So these Croats were treated as prisoners of war and were later exchanged for those Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And were they kept separately from the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were always kept separately from the Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you would have them in two separate rooms? You mentioned the preparation of certain rooms and, whereas other rooms were in a better condition. You always ensured that they were in separate rooms, then? The Croats and the Serbs, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never allowed, Your Honours, for them to be together in a single room because of security considerations. And throughout the period of the war, it never happened that Serb and Croat inmates would be in the same room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What year was this and what month was this, when you had these people in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was perhaps May or June 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these people who were transferred to this hospital, how long had they been detained for in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how long they had been detained in Golubici. In Golubic I never saw them in fact, and I said previously that I didn't know how long they had been detained. I believe not long. Perhaps they were transferred to Knin on the same day, because, had they been there for a longer time, I would probably know where they were, in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what I can't understand, that you don't even know that they were transferred the same day. You were in Golubic, yourself? You were only called for five days or so after they had been transferred. How did you know when they came to Golubic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why should I know? I was training these other people. It was not me who captured them. Someone had captured them, and taken them to Golubic. I actually had no reason to know that they had been captured and brought to Golubic. I only saw those people for the first time at the hospital in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there detention facilities at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there are no detention facilities in Golubic. This is a youth settlement, a youth centre, consisting of prefabricated cottages, sheds. And they are spread over a quite large area, and there were some seven or eight of such prefabricated structures there. This is where youth participating in voluntary youth drives during the previous system, the Communist system, stayed and slept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I just didn't want to interrupt, but now you said you were assuming these prisoners were detained in Golubic only for a very short time. Maybe only for one day or less. But before, you identified these prisoners who were to be transferred to Knin Hospital, the old hospital, as the Croat prisoners mentioned before, you said. And that, I understood, as the Croats who were abused at this other occasion, because it hadn't mentioned other Croat prisoners before, except with this incident and then Captain Dragan informed Mr. Martic. Do you remember your testimony? Were they not the same prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: He mentions prisoners at line 13 or detainees, so it could be understood that he was referring to them, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no, I'm -- please, can you answer this question? Were these the same Croats who were or some of them were abused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same men, those same people. It all happened within a couple of days, so after that incident I assumed the idea was to move them to Knin, to some separate building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So now it's a couple of days, not one day. It must have been more than one day according to what you are telling me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, try to be a little more focused with your answers. You said before you were trying to be precise, but you aren't really very precise. Okay. I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said, after about ten days, a replacement came, a replacement came in the form of Territorial Defence men who came to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said they were not so young men from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But the men who originally brought the captives to the old hospital in Knin, all left and only you stayed out of the original group. Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the new commanding officer from the Territorial Defence was not very experienced and he didn't feel capable of handling it himself. So I was asked to stay on and help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did you help out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay together with the Territorial Defence detail that secured those rooms in the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long they stayed. Maybe 15, 20 days or so. Maybe even not that long. It's difficult for me to say, and I don't want to guess too much because the Trial Chamber has already reprimanded me for not being precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time that we are discussing now, were there any prisons in Knin? Was there a regular prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said a moment ago that that was precisely our problem, that there was no prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until the outbreak of the conflict, where would prisoners be placed, if somebody was taken into custody by the Knin police, where would they be taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not on the police force before and I was lucky enough never to be arrested, but I suppose the prisoners were taken to Sibenik, because Sibenik was the closest town to Knin that had a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Risto Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you work together with him on a common assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was that assignment? What did you do with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So when the Territorial Defence detail was there, he called me up and told me that his ministry, Ministry of Justice and Administration was taking charge, taking control of all the prisons, including that one, so he asked me to come and see him and he told me that he had just been appointed minister of justice and administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So did you go and see him and what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to see him and we discussed what needed to be done and that it needed to be done as efficiently as possible and, on that occasion, I suggested that it would be best to hire men who had worked in prisons before, who were trained and qualified for prison work. For instance, there were former prison staff of Serb ethnicity with experience who had been dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you suggest that solution to the minister of justice? Why did you think as it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing happened that moved me to suggest that. There was one guard from that Territorial Defence detail who stood guard at the gate, and once, when I came, he was not there. And I asked, why he wasn't there. And I was told that he had taken a Croat prisoner and went to town. I was already getting anxious, and sent people to look for him. However, he returned on his own, half an hour later. And when I asked where he had been, he told me that he had been to his apartment and he had taken that prisoner so that the prisoner could use the telephone in his apartment to call his family. Which of course is not inhumane, but it's also not allowed to take prisoners out of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. But lest I forget, let me just clear one point. When was this when you were discussing with Mr. Risto Matkovic on the people that you need, the people that were supposed to be guarding now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, now we are talking about the time when the Territorial Defence detail was providing security at the prison. They were there as security detail for a very short time. So it was maybe halfway through that time. Maybe the Territorial Defence detail had been there six or seven days before I had that discussion. I believe it was June, end June 1991. But I really am not that good with dates. I'm not sure. It could have been a little earlier or a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much. We will take a short break and come back at half past 12. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned Mr. Risto Matkovic and the reason why you approached him. Did you reach an agreement with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I had suggested to him to hire people with experience and who had worked in prisons before on the territory of Croatia and had been expelled just because they were Serbs. Of course he said it was an excellent solution, and he accepted my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about your own status at the prison, about your entire arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him I did not have any ambitions to be the warden, that he should find somebody else for that position, and finally I didn't even have the proper training or qualifications for that job. Under our law, warden had to have a degree in law. He asked me to stay on until new staff begins to work, to stay on until I could meet them and they could start in their new jobs and then we would talk later, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you to stay on. To stay on where? And did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me to stay on in the position of prison warden. He appointed me prison warden and I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say Mr. Risto Matkovic, as Minister of Justice, appointed you prison warden, but of which prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district prison in Knin, that was its official name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember had he that was, in which period of the year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already the beginning of August, I believe, 1991. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you succeed in hiring professional prison staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a large measure, yes. I believe 20 people with experience applied, but that was too little for us, because that job required four shifts and we needed six to seven men per shift, so we needed a total of up to 30. And I believe a total of 19 applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said Mr. Matkovic appointed you warden of the district prison. Did the district prison have a chief of the guard detail?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guard detail was supposed to have a chief. We found out one of the applicants had worked in Zagreb, and had a university degree, which was a requirement for the position of warden, and we designated him as a possible -- as a potential chief of the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you establish contact with those people you were hiring? Was it an open competition for those vacancies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no time for such competitions. It spread by word of mouth that there were vacancies. One would find out and he would tell others, and Mr. Matkovic told me that once they come to the prison we would issue them with the appropriate letters of appointment to that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those people who on the instructions of Mr. Matkovic applied to you, did they receive proper decisions, letters of appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until what time was Jovica Novakovic chief of the guard? Can you tell us at least roughly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around the New Year, a couple of days earlier or a couple of days later, perhaps. So before the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you served as warden of the district prison and Jovica Novakovic was chief of the guard in the district prison in Knin, under whose jurisdiction was that prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and Administration, that is the minister himself. It was the minister who had the right to appoint the warden and the deputy warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After that, did the ministry of the interior have any jurisdiction over the district prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at all. It's a completely different ministry and had no jurisdiction whatsoever over the district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now see on the screen one document, namely Exhibit 906. Can we zoom in on the left top corner? See it more clearly, the heading. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read to us, where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republic of Serbia and Krajina, district prison, Knin". So somebody from the district prison of Knin wrote it and it was addressed to the ministry for justice and administration. I suppose it was the warden who sent it to the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we just raise it a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm probably having a different exhibit here. I've got nothing about Republic of Serbia and Krajina. I just have "authorised by the chief of administration, Milan Babic. Rule book". Is that it? Then I've got the wrong thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour for drawing our attention to that. We have this document on our screen. Seeing the B/C/S, it is a document of the district prison in Knin. Quite different one. It's from the 19th of May, 1993. As it is from the 65 ter list, it should also exist in the English version. It has been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Apparently only one part of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now I have something in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. The letter is in B/C/S and the rule book is in both languages. They belong together, is the impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is an English translation of this document, and it is -- it starts at page 9 of the English document that was on the screen before. So it does -- it follows the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope I can get the other document back now on my screen. I'm afraid, Mr. Whiting, page 9 of that document gives us a page that is cut out in columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It starts there at the bottom of the page. That's the beginning of the document, at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now we have lost the document in the B/C/S version, so we need to have that restored on our screens. That is okay. Can we zoom in on the document so that the witness could look at the line 3 from the top. You said a while ago that this was a document of the district prison in Knin. That will do. Thank you. You can stop now. And the serial number 1, which indicates the name of a person, there are three words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says a list of all workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We now on the English need to go to the next page, to follow along. Turn to page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this document of the district prison in Knin, does it refer to a list of workers employed in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. But this is a somewhat later period, when I was not the warden. But this person under number 1 Nikola Ljubojevic was. So he was submitting a list of workers to the new minister, probably, because Mr. Matkovic was no longer the Minister of Justice. So that this new minister was probably asking for a list of the employed, of the prison staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Can we look at page 3 in B/C/S, that being the number 10. So this is a list of workers from 1 to 10. So we can see the person under number 10, which in the B/C/S version is on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's Page 12 on the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if the witness could see this page 3, it's 6277 in the B/C/S version. That is in the top right corner. To save time, Your Honours, I can give the witness a hard copy text for him to consult. It is just that you won't be aware that he is looking at page 3 in the B/C/S, but by your leave, I shall do so, in order to save time, because now we've lost the B/C/S page -- no, it is back. We shall go through it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the first paragraph from the top, please. Will you read out for us the particulars given for this person under 10.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Stevo Plejo, father Marko, born on the 15th of June, 1964 in Rasinja municipality of Knin. Completed elementary education in Kosovo and secondary mechanical engineering school in Knin. Mechanical technician by occupation. So far has worked at the Tvik in Knin and started working in the district prison on the 17th of August, 1991. Has a total of eight years of working service. Stevo lives with his parents in his family home in Rasinja and has been working as the operator of basic records of the main register in the district prison in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On behalf of the interpreter, I must protest that you guys are very fast. Please slow down. Sorry, Mr. Plejo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was reading his own record, that is why he went through it so quickly, and he has apologised, and I apologise on his behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this person under 10, that is you, Mr. Plejo. You are indicated as working in the district prison in Knin as of the 17th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that you were also the keeper of the central register, of the central records, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When it says here that you were the keeper of the central register, whose records were those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the district prison in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can now remove this document from the screen. We no longer need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, there seems to be a discrepancy between the paragraph 9 that is on the document and what was read by the interpreter towards the end. Some of what is on the transcript is not on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for this warning. Can I ask the witness by leave to read this again slowly? Or to confirm that the data given under item 10 actually does refer to him? I'm not quite sure whether I understood your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She was looking at the wrong passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I must confess. My apologies are in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I stand corrected. It is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Jovica Novakovic was the chief of the guard service in the district prison of Knin until the end of 1991 or early 1992 and who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After him, Ilija Tauz occupied that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was that person, and why did he come? Was there a specific reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Tauz worked in the district prison in Zagreb. He was the chief of the guards there. And because of the goings on in Croatia, I believe that he had been retired early. At any rate, they had gotten rid of all Serbs in all the prisons in whatever way. The way wasn't important. I'm sorry, what was your second question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said Mr. Tauz was the chief of the guards in the district prison in Zadar. How did he come to be hired in the Knin district prison. He was a retired worker you say. Did he accept this gladly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him to accept this position. I was not happy with the work of the previous chief of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask that of him in your capacity of warden of the district prison? Or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe your question may clear up my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said you were not happy with his work and you were looking for a different person. In what capacity were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. I've omitted something. I was not happy with his work, and I went to see the minister, and I told him that I was not satisfied with his work and I explained why I was not satisfied with it. Having heard me, the minister, and I'm referring to minister Matkovic, having heard my reasons, he said that: No problem. I shall replace him, because he was the only person that could replace him. I couldn't do that. But before that, we have to find another man, and I've heard of Mr. Tauz that he worked in Zadar as -- that he was very strict chief of the guards while steady head of that service. He was a very good professional. So I looked him up at the instructions of Mr. Matkovic and I asked him to come -- I asked him whether he wanted to come and be chief of guards in our prison in Knin. Well, he waivered for a while. He wouldn't accept it readily, but I thought that I would be able to persuade him. So I went to see the minister again. I gave him this telephone number and the minister called him up and told him to come and see him in his -- the minister's office. And Mr. Tauz did so and, probably with the greater authority that he wielded, Mr. Matkovic managed to persuade him to assume this post as the chief of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But you have to answer my question. Why were you not satisfied with the work of Jovica Novakovic, the chief of the guards, and you were the warden of the prison there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was appointed chief of the guards, I told him that it was his duty to be in charge of the guards and to only mind the guard business. He had free reign as far as that was concerned from me. I told him: Should any guard misbehave in the sense of violating our law, the law, the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions, that was the name of the law, he should, by all means, come to me and I will take the necessary steps, meaning punishment, suspension, dismissal, et cetera. But he didn't abide by this. I was once informed that two guards had not treated some prisoners, were slapping them about in his presence. He wasn't doing the slapping, but he was present and did nothing to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have explained that he didn't do anything to prevent it, but did he inform you about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't even inform me about it, and I got this from a different source, this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come by such information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was my custom to tour the premises, the rooms in which the prisoners were being held in custody, and it was also my custom to go into the rooms and talk to those people and they would confide in me if they had been -- if anything had been remiss they would inform me about it. And I had the habit of going into the rooms and talking to the people directly myself. And they told me that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this particular case, did you also relate it in this way to Mr. Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And he agreed that a new chief of the guards should be placed in the stead, that the old chief of the guards should be replaced by a new one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did Mr. Tauz assume his post in the district prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was early in January, 1992. The former chief was automatically -- immediately, rather, replaced and several days thereafter Mr. Tauz showed up for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you follow the work of Mr. Tauz as chief of the guards and were you satisfied with it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did follow his work and I was absolutely happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is -- what are you guided by when you say that you were absolutely happy with his work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him the same thing that I had told the previous chief of guards, that he had only to keep tabs on the guard, to control the guard. Everything else, material supplies, medical requirements, clothing, vehicles, all such requirements were my duty and I would see to that; that his only task was to be a chief of the guards by the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the duty of the guards in the district prison of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the particular post, but the task of the guards were to perform their duty in keeping with the law on the enforcement of criminal and misdemeanor sanctions. If you want me to say something very concrete to secure the prison building, to escort people to trial, or to escort people deprived of their freedom to hospital, if that was necessary, and such other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the Knin district prison in the time under review, were there house rules that were applicable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we drew up house rules list, which was an in-house list of rules to be abided by in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did those house rules prescribe which staff members had which duties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you were happy with the work of Mr. Tauz, does it mean he worked differently than the previous chief of guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was much stricter with his guards and if an incident would happen, he would, as a rule, immediately inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you received notification of an incident, what was your duty and what were the duties of others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to institute disciplinary proceedings against the person, the offender, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did such proceedings actually take place while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe ten cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of offences gave rise to such proceedings? I don't mean the names of offenders, but what kind of offences?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Failure to report regularly for the shift and excessive use of force. Those were the two most common reasons, although there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were those disciplinary proceedings like? What possibilities were open to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had forgotten to mention that the warden of the prison had set up and appointed the disciplinary commission complete with a chairman, and this disciplinary panel or commission would handle the proceedings. However, if the warden of the prison was unhappy with the decision of the panel, he had the last word. He would take the final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By warden, you mean yourself? When you say the warden had a disciplinary commission and if the warden was not happy with the decision, the warden decided himself. This warden is yourself? It was yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What measures were available to the disciplinary panel under the law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reprimand; fine deductible from the salary; suspension, that is temporary removal from work; and finally dismissal, depending on the gravity of the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to actually take all of these kinds of measures?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you remember that one of the offences against roles of service was, in your words, excessive use of force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did excessive use of force mean, in a prison environment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law on the execution of punishment for criminal and offences and misdemeanors prescribed that a guard was allowed to use force only against a prisoner who was offering resistance, and in no other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe that rule and did your employees do the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did and those among my staff who did not were subjected to disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said one of the possibilities was suspension. What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that meant temporary removal from work. And you know how it goes. Later on, we would look at all of the options and what can be done, whether there were other guards available for hire. Then the offender would be dismissed. If there was no alternative staff member, then the offender would be reinstituted three or six months later after receiving a strict caution never to repeat the offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does what you say mean that maltreatment of detained persons was absolutely prohibited by the law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The guards were only required to observe the law and house rules and the law on criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was your conduct at the district prison in Knin supervised by any authority?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was already the beginning of 1992 and almost every week we would have representatives of the International Red Cross visiting the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did ICRC representatives actually have access to the prisoners? Could they talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They always had the opportunity to talk to them, sometimes they would come announced, sometimes unannounced. But no matter what, we would always give them access to the prisoners and they could talk with them unsupervised by the staff. They could talk to the prisoners without any of the staff members of the prison being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did ICRC representatives supply you, as the warden, with copies of their findings or reports after making such interviews with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they completed their tour of the prison, they would come to see me. They would never give me any copies of reports or findings, but they would verbally share their comments with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were those comments about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all of them had to do with the material side of things. I had a hard time explaining to them that whatever difficulties we had in the prison concerning hygiene and some other things, they were common to the rest of the population, outside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that hygiene was the greatest problem?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if prisoners had access to the bathroom twice a week, they would require it four times a week. But it was difficult. The technical possibilities available did not allow us to meet their requirements, but whenever we could, we did. We had only two bathrooms in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 905. Could we see the left top copy, close-up, so the witness can read it. Can you see what kind of document this is, Mr. Plejo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of employees of the district prison of Knin, including the positions. It's basically a list of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we just see the end of the document as well. All of it. We see there is headings, various titles of staff: Supervisors, senior guards, guards, junior guards and last, policemen. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do these titles actually reflect the actual positions held by staff for the district prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of these people actually worked at the prison, with the proviso that you have two categories of guards: Guards and junior guards, or guards on a trial period. I already explained that we had a shortage of guards. These guards on the trial period were people who had completed secondary education, but did not complete specialised course for guards. And in category five were policemen who had worked previously as policemen in Croatia but had been dismissed. Let's look for instance at number 1, Vujo Kusalo. That was precisely his case. And the others, together with him, had expressed their wish to work at the district prison in Knin. And I thought it made more sense to hire an experienced policeman rather than somebody in category 5. In other words, I preferred to hire a professional policeman than, let's say, a carpenter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On this date, the date of 19th of October, 1992, were you normally employed at this place? Were you normally the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which date, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1992. If you look at the first page of this document, the "Republic of Serbia Krajina, Knin district prison, Knin, 19 October, 1992". On that date, were you still the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible. Sometime around that time I stopped working as warden. Maybe in March or April, 1992 a new warden came, a man we had found, Nikola Ljubojevic who had earlier worked in the Lepoglava prison. And now we come back to what I said earlier when I said to the minister that I was not really eager to work as a warden. And I stayed on until we found somebody. So we found this Nikola Ljubojevic who had worked in Lepoglava prison. However he left only two days later for some family reason. His daughter had found an apartment in Serbia and the minister, again, asked me to stay on until we found a new warden. So for a while, maybe from March 1992 until April I was acting warden. That is from March or April until August 1992. And only in August was I replaced by Nikola Lubavice [as interpreted] as a warden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The first one was Nikola Ljubojevic and now it is Nikola Lubavice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning this, Mr. Milovancevic, because I don't see a warden listed on this list. And this is a list of employees of the Knin district prison and it doesn't mention a warden. It doesn't mention the position. It doesn't mention the person employed as a warden. That's the only reason I was asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I may assist the Trial Chamber. In Serbia, sometimes we make a distinction between worker and employee. This is a list of workers, and the warden is an employee of the prison. That is a slight linguistic difference, that's why he is not listed as a worker. I hope I have helped you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So guards, supervisors, like Mr. Ilija Tauz would be regarded a worker, not an employee? Mr. Milovancevic or Witness, can you answer that question? The guard supervisor who is contained in this list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask, sir? I've already said earlier that warden is a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, that is not my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- subject to an appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The guard supervisor, I was referring to Ilija Tauz who is the number 1 on this list, you may see it still on the screen. My question was, if this position of the guard supervisor in this case was the position of an employee or of a worker. Do you know the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both worker and employee. Well, in my book it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: For you it seems to be the same, but you are not a lawyer yourself, so it's a term of labour law, of course, and I didn't want to ask you any legal question. But so it is not such a common distinction as it is in some countries. In my country we have this distinction between employees and workers and in other countries they reformed that by calling everybody employees. You don't make that difference in daily life probably, so you cannot really answer that question, can you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask now question. Mr. Plejo, you indicated that Jovica Novakovic was the chief guard until end of 1991, early 1992 and he was replaced by Ilija Tauz, but he's listed here with Ilija Tauz as of October 1992, as both supervisors. Both of them are supervisors. You realise that? So he really didn't replace Jovica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says supervisors here, which are titles like a first-class police officer, or I don't know how it is with you, but the chief of the guards is elected from among the supervisors. There can be 50 supervisors or superintendents, but one, only one of them shall be elected to be the chief of the guards. The chief of the guards service would be the best one from among them. So here it says supervisors, so that is more like a rank, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The chief of these among the supervisors was elected by the Minister of Justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Didn't -- again, you may correct me here -- didn't you say that after you complained to the minister that Jovica Novakovic be dismissed, that you then went and looked for a replacement and that Ilija Tauz had been -- had been resigned or dismissed in Croatia and he had experience. And you looked for him and you brought him in to come and replace Jovica Novakovic. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that I was not satisfied with him and Jovica Novakovic was replaced, having been suspended from work for a while. And then Ilija Tauz was appointed in his stead. Novakovic was reinstated later, but in a lower position. He never was the warden or the chief of the prison, the chief of the guards. As regards their actual ranks, I could not strip them of their ranks or promote them to a higher one. These are the ranks indicated here, the day acquired, their schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we are talking at cross-purposes. My understanding of your testimony was that Jovica Novakovic was the chief of the guards until the -- you said in your own words, end 1991, early 1992, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said that because you were not happy, you got him dismissed. Then you had to go and look for a replacement and you found out that Ilija Tauz had left his job in Croatia. I don't know whether dismissed or resigned. That's why I say "left." And then you brought him in. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, but I did not say that Jovica Novakovic had been dismissed. He had been replaced as chief of the prison. And he was reinstated in a lower position. The designations which appear here, this is only with reference to their salaries, under Roman numeral 1, it says supervisors, rather than chief of the prison guards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chief of prison, you meant also chief of the guards, before? Just a minute ago you said chief of the prison. You were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I meant, right. So I meant, when I said the chief of the prison, I meant the chief of the prison guards, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me try to put my question again. Are you saying -- or let me find out. When Jovica was replaced as chief of the guards, he was not dismissed? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not laid off. He was not dismissed. He had only been suspended from work for a while, and was later given a lower position. No longer the position of the chief of the guards, but he occupied a lower position and had duties pertaining to that lower rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. I am not finding what I am looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We shall try to obtain an answer, Mr. Plejo. These remarks under Roman numerals, one, two, three, four and five, are these -- what are these designations of ranks or titles of specific functions in the prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are ranks, like in the army when you have a General or a Colonel, these are the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under Roman numeral one, we have the supervisors of the guard. And do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These are -- there are three names there. Is this fact that Jovica Novakovic is indicated as a guard supervisor, does it mean that he is the warden, the chief of the prison guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the prison guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Tauz was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that from among these three guard supervisors, the minister was to decide which one would be appointed as chief of the prison guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it means. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how else to try to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you will -- you have to elect the chief of the prison guards not from among the probationers but from among those with the next highest rank and I hope that that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask one thing which is not yet clear to me. We were talking about the time when this document was produced. This was in, I think, late August 1992, wasn't it? Then you explained that you were maybe yourself at this time no warden any more. Could you explain to us if you then left this position and never came back as a warden or in any function in this prison? Or was it only a short term programme and then you continued working there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I explained a while ago that I asked the minister, it not being my ambition to be the prison warden, I asked the minister to find a solution, to find a person to appoint to that position, the position of prison warden. This was in March or April 1992, a man by the name of Nikola Kukavica was appointed prison warden. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. You then explained about this interim period where you were acting chief or acting warden, until August and this was then -- and then continue with for the rest of the period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when Kukavica left for reasons known to him, the minister reappointed me, or rather, he asked me to serve in the interim period as acting prison warden until he found the right person. So for another two or three months, I was acting prison warden until Nikola Ljubojevic came, who was then appointed prison warden, and this was perhaps on the -- in September or October 1992. And since that time I worked as the keeper of the central records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In the same institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How long did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue. That saves us some time, you know. This is why I'm asking these questions now, as it's in connection with the others. Please, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one question. Would this document reflect the demotion of Jovica Novakovic and what rank would he have been demoted to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not what this document states. This is just a list of workers by rank. This document does not indicate the actual work posts of the persons indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. So what rank was he demoted to? You mentioned the fact that he was suspended for a while and then he was returned to work and demoted, I believe. Sorry. You mentioned -- let me repeat. That he was suspended for a while and then returned to work and demoted. Is that not the evidence? So I am asking, what rank was he demoted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've explained that I couldn't either promote or demote him, in terms of his rank. I could give him a lower position within the prison structure. He no longer was the chief of the prison guards. I just gave him a lower work post within the prison structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Point taken. What lower position did he receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a supervisor in charge of a group or to escort people to court. There is a job description that corresponded to his rank, but he no longer was the chief of the prison guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the house rules like in prison? Where was there avail? What about the meals, baths, medical care? Let me not put to you all of the specific questions. Can you just give us a brief description?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely what was prescribed by the house rules. We would get up in the morning at 6 o'clock, have breakfast at 7. There were three meals: Breakfast, lunch and dinner. And we were served meals as everybody else. They were served meals, the same meals as the employed. The baths would be taken twice a week, as far as I can remember. And the doctor came occasionally to visit; I believe, initially, twice a week. And later we hired a medical nurse who was on the permanent staff and was there on all day duty. If the doctor only prescribed some therapy for some patients, if he felt that that was necessary, he would do so and he would also order persons taken to hospital, if he thought such treatment was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that the prisoners did not make their own food, but that it was supplied to them, what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supplied to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was that food prepared?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially we received food from all over the place, as it were. We sometimes asked the army to give us food, and then the police. And later, we set up our own kitchen and hired, I believe, two lady cooks and actually equipped the entire kitchen to be able to cater to our own needs and we had professional chefs employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kinds of uniforms did the prison guards have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they mainly wore their own, because we were not -- because of the -- our financial constraints which prevented us from buying them, so special uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said something that might be confusing, and you said something which might be misconstrued. What do you mean "in their own". What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that they wore the clothing that they had at the moment of detention. They would wear what they had at the moment of detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you didn't understand my question. I didn't ask you what were the uniforms of the inmates, but of the guards. That is what I asked.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards wore blue uniforms, mainly uniforms like those worn before the war by prison guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those uniforms identical to the policemen's uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not identical to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: For a while you were the keeper of the central records. Does that mean that the prison maintained the central records unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did a detainee or a person on the premises of the prison have to have of documents? Did they have to hold any documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person had to have a decision from the competent court covering his detention, accounting for his detention. If it was a petty offence, that would be a decision issued by the municipal petty offences or misdemeanors court. In cases of criminal offences, then it would be a decision of the district court in Knin or another competent court. At any rate, every person, every inmate had to have a document accounting for his or her detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who decided whether someone would be placed in the premises of the Knin district prison?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Courts made such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you admit someone to hospital -- or to prison, sorry, and release him from prison on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC [Resumed]
